title: All one (Galatians 3:26–28)
hook: neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female

segments.voice: Yesterday, hilaros: God loveth a cheerful giver. Your line was cheerful. Did your gift come with a real smile? Day five hundred eighty.

In the story Acts tells, the first followers of Jesus were Jews. Then Gentiles began to believe too, and a hard question split the young movement. Did a Gentile have to become Jewish first, be circumcised and take on the law of Moses, to belong fully? In the churches of Galatia, in what's now central Turkey, teachers were saying yes. Paul, a Jew himself and proud of it, was saying no. The letter to the Galatians is the heat of that argument. And in the middle of it, Paul writes a sentence that still startles.
screen: `JEWS FIRST, THEN GENTILES.` → `MUST THEY BECOME JEWISH FIRST?` → `A STARTLING SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: He starts with what makes someone belong: "For you are all the children of God by faith, in Christ Jesus." Then baptism: "For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ." Put on, like clothing. And then: "There is neither Jew nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free: there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus." Those three pairs were lines that divided the world Paul lived in: people, status, sex. Notice the third pair is worded differently from the first two. In the Greek it reads, literally, no male and female: the words of Genesis, where God creates them male and female. Paul is reaching back to creation. And notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the differences vanish. In his letters he still writes to slaves and masters, husbands and wives, Jews and Greeks, as who they are. What he says is that in Christ none of these decides who belongs, or who ranks higher. The word one, in Greek, is masculine: not one thing, a blend, but one person, as if all of them together were one new man in Christ. Catholics see this at the font. In the rite of baptism, the newly baptized is clothed in a white garment, a sign that they have put on Christ. A child, an elderly convert, a prince, a refugee: the same water, the same white cloth. Christians have taken centuries, and are still taking them, to live out what this sentence says.
screen: `CHILDREN OF GOD BY FAITH.` · `BAPTIZED: YOU HAVE PUT ON CHRIST.` · `NO MALE AND FEMALE: GENESIS.` · `ONE: NOT A BLEND, ONE PERSON.` · then, large: `YOU ARE ALL ONE IN CHRIST JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who you rank. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people you'll see today: at home, at work, on the bus, the person who serves your coffee. Go through them slowly. Notice who you automatically put higher, and who lower. Who you'd listen to first, and who you barely see. Don't scold yourself. Just notice. Then picture them all wearing the same white garment, standing at the same font. If you pray, you can pray for the ones you usually overlook. If you don't, simply hold them all in the same light for a moment. The bell holds the time.
All one. Paul's sentence to the Galatians: neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, but all one in Christ Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: all one in christ. Today, give the person you usually overlook the same attention you'd give the person you most want to impress. Day five hundred eighty.

howItsDone: In the Catholic rite of baptism, the newly baptized is clothed in a white garment as a sign of having put on Christ; the same rite is used for every person, whatever their rank.

original.note: Greek: one, in the masculine form. Galatians 3:28: not 'one thing' but 'one' person in Christ.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slogan that says everyone's the same.
what it means: in Christ, peoples, status and sex no longer decide who belongs or who ranks higher.
what a scholar hears: the third pair quotes Genesis 1:27 ('male and female'); heis is masculine, one person, not a blend.

notes: Framing of the Galatian dispute: described as an internal question among Jesus's followers, with Paul as a Jew; Jewish law is not used as a foil. Confirm tone.
Greek of 3:28 'ouk eni arsen kai thēly' echoing Genesis 1:27 LXX: a common scholarly observation. Confirm.
White garment in the rite of baptism: CCC 1243. Confirm.
'Christians have taken centuries... to live out' this sentence: a soft, general historical remark. Confirm acceptable.
